canonical_definition:
What it is. Across the surveyed work, BIG-Bench Hard is most commonly described as a challenging subset of BIG-Bench used for reasoning-focused evaluation. Most definitions emphasize hard tasks requiring complex or multi-step reasoning, though some also describe it as covering semantic understanding, language understanding, world knowledge, or general language understanding. Papers describe its makeup differently: many refer to 23 tasks, some to 27 tasks or 27 tasks across 23 task types, one to 21 tasks, and one to 23 multiple-choice tasks plus 4 free-form generation tasks. Some studies use only selected BBH tasks or categories, such as DATE, Navigate, Boolean Expression, Dyck Language, or sports_understanding, rather than the full suite.

What it is claimed to measure. Papers link BBH to 20 constructs and 12 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure reasoning, with recurring construct claims around general ability and generalization, while other construct claims are more dispersed. On the behavioral side, the most recurrent named uses are complex reasoning question answering and instruction following, and the remaining 10 indicators are spread across other behaviors. Overall, papers cluster their measurement claims around reasoning but also use BBH for a broader mix of capability claims.

Space of uses. Papers often use BBH inside multi-benchmark evaluation suites, commonly alongside MMLU, and they run it in zero-shot, 3-shot, many-shot in-context learning, or chain-of-thought settings, sometimes on selected subtasks and sometimes with exact-match scoring. In the recorded relationship language, Open LLM Leaderboard and BIG-Bench Logical Deduction are measured by BBH, BBH is measured by lm-evaluation-harness, and BBH is related to LiveBench.

Concerns raised. Explicit concerns are limited. A single paper treats BBH as only multiple-choice and adds Alpaca to show generalization to open-ended generation tasks, while other papers describe BBH as including free-form generation or mixed multiple-choice and exact-match tasks, so papers do not fully agree on its output format. Another paper relates BBH to LiveBench by describing LiveBench as containing "harder, contamination-limited versions" of tasks from earlier benchmarks such as BBH.

characterization_sections.label: What it is.
characterization_sections.text: Across the surveyed work, BIG-Bench Hard is most commonly described as a challenging subset of BIG-Bench used for reasoning-focused evaluation. Most definitions emphasize hard tasks requiring complex or multi-step reasoning, though some also describe it as covering semantic understanding, language understanding, world knowledge, or general language understanding. Papers describe its makeup differently: many refer to 23 tasks, some to 27 tasks or 27 tasks across 23 task types, one to 21 tasks, and one to 23 multiple-choice tasks plus 4 free-form generation tasks. Some studies use only selected BBH tasks or categories, such as DATE, Navigate, Boolean Expression, Dyck Language, or sports_understanding, rather than the full suite.

characterization_sections.label: What it is claimed to measure.
characterization_sections.text: Papers link BBH to 20 constructs and 12 behavioral indicators. The prevailing use is to measure reasoning, with recurring construct claims around general ability and generalization, while other construct claims are more dispersed. On the behavioral side, the most recurrent named uses are complex reasoning question answering and instruction following, and the remaining 10 indicators are spread across other behaviors. Overall, papers cluster their measurement claims around reasoning but also use BBH for a broader mix of capability claims.

characterization_sections.label: Space of uses.
characterization_sections.text: Papers often use BBH inside multi-benchmark evaluation suites, commonly alongside MMLU, and they run it in zero-shot, 3-shot, many-shot in-context learning, or chain-of-thought settings, sometimes on selected subtasks and sometimes with exact-match scoring. In the recorded relationship language, Open LLM Leaderboard and BIG-Bench Logical Deduction are measured by BBH, BBH is measured by lm-evaluation-harness, and BBH is related to LiveBench.

characterization_sections.label: Concerns raised.
characterization_sections.text: Explicit concerns are limited. A single paper treats BBH as only multiple-choice and adds Alpaca to show generalization to open-ended generation tasks, while other papers describe BBH as including free-form generation or mixed multiple-choice and exact-match tasks, so papers do not fully agree on its output format. Another paper relates BBH to LiveBench by describing LiveBench as containing "harder, contamination-limited versions" of tasks from earlier benchmarks such as BBH.
